8: This paper will examine, using existing case studies and research, how Bitcoin mining could be an important catalyst for climate action in each of these four categories.
13: To date, despite the improved studies on Bitcoin mining, they have tended to appear only in academic journals. These may be inaccessible to the general public, or to those not familiar with how grid infrastructure or methane mitigation works. Specifically, there has not yet been an evidence-based article that tries to objectively bring together the different ways Bitcoin supports, or could in the future support, climate action. This article makes a first humble attempt to do so. It uses a combination of peer reviewed research sources, case studies and [[7|Whitepapers]] to come up with an overall perspective on how Bitcoin is, and could in the future, promote Climate Action.
17: **Interconnection Queues** Lengthy interconnection queues delay renewable projects from connecting to the grid. Reasons for delay include old transmission infrastructure, regulatory bottlenecks, limited grid capacity and lack of financing for the renewable project. Grid operators are also concerned about the impact of more intermittent power sources on the grid. These delays can be [[8|as long as 10-15 years]], slowing the renewable transition, and compromising our net zero emission goals.
18: **Wasted Renewable Energy and Curtailment** Intermittent renewable generation often exceeds grid demand, forcing renewable operators to curtail excess energy. Curtailment can have [[9|far-reaching consequences]], hurting not only the financial viability of renewable projects but also grid stability. It also hurts economically. The grid operator must often [[11|pay the renewable generator a fee]] for not being able to take their energy, and those added costs are often [[10|being handed on to consumers]]. Australia for example is currently [[12|wasting 25%]] of all renewable energy. Such waste slows down the renewable transition both directly and indirectly. Directly, it reduces the profits, and so the expansion-speed, of renewable operators. Indirectly, it gives fuel to [[13|opponents of renewable energy]] to question the viability of the renewable transition itself.
19: **Create more demand-side flexibility** Variable Renewable Energy such as solar and wind generation requires electrical grids to balance variable supply with adaptable demand. Lack of flexible demand (industries that can adjust usage) or [[14|demand response]] programs results in grid instability. That makes it harder to justify expanding renewables without risking grid reliability. Flexible consumers give grid operators the confidence to increase the amount of variable renewable energy generation on a grid, knowing they have a demand-side shock-absorber in place.
26: In Ethiopia, the Electric Power Agency has welcomed Bitcoin miners to buy excess energy from the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD). This is powering growth and green energy, and has earned the country [[15|$55M in 10 months]]. The country is using that money to build out more transmission capacity to deliver more renewable energy.
27: The scientific community agrees. By reducing the financial and logistical barriers to renewable energy deployment, Bitcoin mining speeds up the adoption of clean energy. This finding is supported by [[16|You et al]], 2023 __(Mining to Mitigation: How Bitcoin Can Support Renewable Energy Development and Climate Action)__ and [[17|Menati et al]], 2023 __(High resolution modeling and analysis of cryptocurrency mining’s impact on power grids)__.
29: In Texas, there have been many cases of underused solar or wind farms. For example, in 2022 Compute North (now US Bitcoin Corp) purchased a [[18|280 wind farm in West Texas]]. The farm had been known for high curtailment fees, from wind that the grid could not use due to weak demand. By providing a guaranteed customer for that surplus wind energy, the Bitcoin facility reduced waste, ended curtailment fees, and helped stabilize the grid. Also on the ERCOT (Electric Reliability Council of Texas) grid, Bitcoin mining company Jiachi West [[19|began operating in Texas]]. It reported that renewable energy curtailment dropped by 4%, and renewable energy profitability increased by 12%.
33: But these are not just academic theoretical possibilities. Indeed academia has lagged behind a large volume of real-world projects. These have already integrated Bitcoin mining with renewable energy in order to improve the payback time.
34: For example, [[21|Deutsche Telecom]], Germany's largest telco, has begun using Bitcoin mining to monetize its otherwise wasted wind and solar power. It hopes to use the increased revenue to make solar and wind production more profitable, and reinvest the profits into more renewable generation. [[22|Tepco, Japan's largest Utility]] company, also recently announced a project to begin using Bitcoin mining on its wasted renewable energy. Its goal is to further reduce waste of renewable electricity. Bitcoin mining's time-of-day agnostic properties let it use solar and wind that otherwise would have been curtailed.
35: Saul Griffiths, a leading energy expert and author of [[23|__Electrify__]][[24|: An Optimist's Playbook for Our Clean Energy Future]], argues that flexible energy demand is essential for incentivizing the construction of new renewable energy infrastructure. Traditional industries need a constant and predictable energy supply. Bitcoin mining, by contrast, is highly flexible. Miners can scale their operations up or down in response to energy availability, which makes them ideal partners for renewable energy producers.
36: This flexibility creates a symbiotic relationship between Bitcoin miners and renewable energy developers. For example, during periods of low energy demand (e.g., sunny afternoons or windy nights), miners can ramp up operations, providing a steady revenue stream for energy producers. During peak demand, miners can power down, freeing up energy for the grid. This helps stabilize the grid and encourages the development of more renewable energy capacity. In places like Norway, where hydropower dominates the energy mix, Bitcoin miners have become key players in balancing supply and demand. They help keep renewable energy profitable and scalable.
37: By improving the economics of renewable energy projects, Bitcoin mining helps unlock the capital needed to build more solar, wind, and hydropower facilities. These real-world examples show that Bitcoin mining is not just a consumer of energy. It is a strategic partner in the global transition to a [[25|sustainable energy]] future.
39: It is by no means the only technology needed to solve the first two challenges. But there is [[26|equally strong evidence]] that it is [[27|the most profitable way]] to reduce both solar/wind payback periods and increase the flexibility of energy consumption.
42: Like eVs, Bitcoin is a fully electrified technology with no direct emissions. Also like eVs, Bitcoin produces secondary emissions, because some of the power used comes from fossil fuel sources. And as with eVs, it is important to remember that this power obviates a more emission-intensive predecessor. For eVs, that is petrol and diesel transport. For Bitcoin, it is banking services and the extractive, fossil-fuel dependent gold industry.
45: In parallel to greening the grid, prominent environmental campaigners and energy experts such as Saul Griffiths in his book [[34|Electrify]] say we must also electrify as many industrial processes as possible. Heating is the single largest candidate for rapid electrification.
46: Bitcoin mining cannot replace the intense heat of a coal furnace. But there are large amounts of other heat that the exhaust heat of Bitcoin miners can replace, and is now replacing. The potential uses for heat from Bitcoin mining are significant and growing. Some of these are one-off applications. Others, such as delivering [[35|district heating]] to 2% of Finland's population, are already operating at a significant scale.
54: **Heating for Horticultur**e: [[47|Bitcoin Brabant]], led by Bert de Groot, has been helping decarbonize the greenhouse industry in the Netherlands. It uses solar-powered Bitcoin mining to deliver heat for the greenhouses, which reduces the industry's reliance on natural gas. There are already [[48|many such greenhouses being heated by Bitcoin mining]]. This use has the potential to scale, helping industrial greenhouses wean themselves off natural-gas based heating.
56: In 2023, Shelter Point Distillery in Campbell River, Canada, created the '[[52|world's first sustainable digital tumbler]]' by attaching a Bitcoin miner to provide heat for the whiskey aging process. Genesis Digital Assets (GDA) launched [[53|a Bitcoin mining heat repurposing project]] in Norsjö, Sweden, using renewable hydro-energy. The recycled heat cuts the cost of keeping snow-cleaning trucks from freezing in an area prone to harsh winters.
61: OTEC however suffered from a lack of funding. It is very expensive to develop new grid-tethered offshore energy generation in the tropics. On top of the challenge that offshore wind faces in supplying power back to the grid, OTEC must also develop hurricane resistance.
62: Bitcoin mining on sea barges removes these constraints by providing a consumer of OTEC energy in situ. This means that the next scale-up R&D effort for OTEC is suddenly economically viable, because the operation will not need the large cost of being grid-tethered and made hurricane-proof. Eventually, the aim of OTEC is to deliver power back to the grid. But Bitcoin mining is playing a critical role in making the scale-up phase of R&D economically viable. Before Bitcoin mining, that R&D had been mothballed since the 1980s.
66: In this [[63|presentation, Erik Hersman]], the founder of Gridless, shows how broken the energy model in Africa is, leaving 600 Million Africans without electricity. He also shows how Bitcoin mining is already starting to unlock untapped renewable energy resources to solve this issue.
69: As humans adapt to Climate Change, getting enough drinking water to arid countries becomes an increasing challenge. There is no one solution, but part of the solution is to make desalination, which is very energy intensive, more cost-effective. MARA, who have also pioneered [[66|Landfill Gas powered]] Bitcoin mining, [[67|home heating]], [[68|flare-gas mitigation]] and [[69|wind-powered]] Bitcoin mining, has begun investing in improving [[70|desalination technology]]. At the same time, it is using Bitcoin mining heat, rather than natural gas, to desalinate water. This results in more water desalination per dollar of energy spent. If scaled, this innovation has the potential to increase water abundance in arid countries.
70: Gas peaker plants, notorious for high emissions and idle-time inefficiencies, are being obviated in Texas thanks to Bitcoin mining’s demand flexibility. Following Winter Storm Uri in 2021, ERCOT interim CEO Brad Jones integrated Bitcoin miners into grid stability programs. By 2024, 3 GW of mining capacity participated in demand response. In a recent report from the Digital Assets Research Institute (DARI), [[71|the data shows]] that Bitcoin mining has now become a critical part of Texas’ ability to grow the share of renewable energy on the grid to meet the needs of its population growth. The ability of Bitcoin miners to curtail usage at peak times was shown to have saved Texas taxpayers $18 Billion, because ERCOT did not need to purchase [[72|highly polluting peaker plants]].
72: Landfills account for 17% of global [[74|methane emissions]], a gas 84x more potent than CO2. Traditional solutions, like flaring or building gas pipelines, are often impractical, because very few commercial operations can co-locate next to a landfill. They can also be very expensive, because the grid must be upgraded to handle the extra electricity. Bitcoin mining offers a breakthrough: mobile mining units can convert vented methane into electricity on-site, eliminating emissions and generating revenue.
75: Gas flaring, which wastes energy while emitting the climate super-warmer methane, persists globally despite World Bank efforts to [[83|stop almost all flaring by 2030]]. To date we have found few ways to make good on that intention. Flaring in regions including the Middle East has recently been shown to cause [[84|more toxic gases than previously feared]].
76: Bitcoin mining is increasingly recognized in independent reports as a potential scalable solution to this problem. Cambridge's April 2025 Bitcoin Mining Report for example called Bitcoin mining a "Potential Solution to Gas Flaring" that shows the "potential for innovation to simultaneously address environmental challenges". It estimated that Bitcoin mining was mitigating [[85|2.2 MT of CO2e emissions per year]].
78: In North Dakota for example, Crusoe’s projects reduced flaring by 99% at partnered sites. Similarly, Upstream Data’s Canadian operations have been cutting flaring since 2017. In another example, climate tech company Unblock Global has achieved [[86|15MW of flare gas powered bitcoin mining]] in Argentina. The company has a mission to eliminate flaring in Latin America, and raised $15 million to use flared gas from Argentina's Vaca Muerta to power its operations. These are three of the [[87|29 Bitcoin mining companies]] that have found a way to solve the 160-year old problem of wasted flare gas. That is why the World Economic Forum [[88|recently praised]] Crusoe's Bitcoin mining operation for helping the UN in its efforts to reduce methane emissions.
81: These Bitcoin mining projects are neither one-offs, nor small. There are [[92|29 Bitcoin mining companies]] that we know of who are carbon negative, using methane emissions as their fuel source. And there are 3 GW of gas peaker plants (that we know of) that have been obviated as a direct result of Bitcoin mining. As the Digital Assets Research Institute [[93|put it]]: “With 3 GW of flexible load resource on the grid, there is no business case for 3 GW of gas peaker plants.”
83: Remarkably, in the last three years Bitcoin mining has shown it can profitably and scalably tackle all three of these thorny environmental challenges. Other energy consumers and conventional gas-capture projects have proven either unprofitable, unscalable or both.
84: Monetizing wasted renewable energy not only speeds up the energy transition but also helps save nature. For example, in East Congo lies Virunga National Park, a 7,800 Km2 terrain that's home to half of Africa's terrestrial species. During COVID the park was threatened with closure. It had lost most of its income, and had no way to pay the staff who protected it from poachers, and from militias who cut down trees for charcoal because of energy shortages in the region.
88: This is not a one-off example. In Costa Rica, Bitcoin mining prevented the loss of 60Ha of land which had been in Eduardo Kopper's family for 5 generations, and financed its [[99|transformation into an eco-sanctuary]]. The model was identical to Virunga: use the otherwise stranded and wasted surplus hydropower to mine Bitcoin onsite, and reinvest the money into saving the land.
89: Critics often assume, without research, "they could have done something else with that stranded energy". Such a view is not only naive. It also diminishes the environmental contributions of stewards of the land such as de Mode in Virunga, DR Congo, and Kopper in Poaz, Costa Rica. Neither of them were Bitcoiners. Both spent years researching what to do with that stranded energy before realizing that Bitcoin mining was their one available option, because it is location-agnostic and time-of-day agnostic.
92: Firstly, for every genuinely bad actor, there have been misreported reports of bad actors that weren't. For example, Greenidge Generation was misreported as opening a gas plant for Bitcoin mining that caused toxic algal blooms in an adjacent lake. It didn't: it opened to provide [[102|power back to the grid]], and there was [[103|no elevated lake temperature]]. Other reports have falsely accused Bitcoin mining companies of raising Texas electricity prices, destabilizing the grid and using excessive water.
93: These claims all turned out to be baseless or based on very poor data. They were also contradicted by studies which reveal that Bitcoin mining in fact has stabilized the grid (see [[104|claim 21]]) and helped [[105|lower electricity prices]] (see [[106|claim 22]]), by reducing curtailment fees while raising grid operator revenues. An anti-Bitcoin reporting bias only turns those in the Bitcoin mining industry against reporters. It also deflects the attention that should be given to genuinely bad actors.
94: The second issue is that those reporting on one-off examples, where Bitcoin mining operations are alleged to have harmed a community, have tended to also take a subjective side-swipe at the entire industry. Time Magazine did this in their Feb 2024 coverage of a Bitcoin mining company's noise levels. More recently, the Cooldown used this same recipe. It added a wholly inaccurate statement to an otherwise accurate piece of reporting on the Thai Bitcoin operation: "Whether done legally or illegally, the [[107|environmental impact]] of cryptocurrency mining cannot be understated." The comment is an example of a side-swipe that ignores the scientific consensus. In this instance, the article cited a [[108|comprehensively debunked outlier study]] on Bitcoin mining to back up the statement. Again, such statements turn the industry against the reporting organization, rather than keeping the focus on what may be a genuine issue worthy of examination.
95: But the third issue is the most severe, because it doesn't just hurt Bitcoin mining but the wider climate movement. Criticism, particularly from Environmental NGOs, has ignored Bitcoin's ability to end gas peaker plant reliance and substantially reduce flaring. That criticism has directly prolonged both the need for [[109|gas peaker plants,]] and the practice of [[110|natural gas flaring]]. (See linked studies for evidence of how NGO criticism of Bitcoin mining has backfired for the Climate movement).
96: It should not be trivialized that Bitcoin mining currently emits [[111|46 Mt CO2-eq of emissions annually]] according to the Digital Assets Research Institute (up from the already significant 41 MT CO2e in 2021). Some in the Bitcoin ecosystem have a habit of saying "But other industries emit much more". That has earned the ire of some in the environmental movement, and rightly so; every industry must take steps to reduce its environmental footprint.
97: Equally, context matters. The photovoltaic (PV) industry, despite its critical role in decarbonizing energy systems, did not achieve a [[112|net-positive carbon balance until 2011]]—57 years after the first solar cell was invented in 1954. PV manufacturing still relies on energy-intensive processes and coal furnaces to melt silicon. Yet it is widely accepted that the photovoltaic industry is net emission reducing, because it now reduces many times more emissions than it creates.
99: More importantly, like EVs, those emissions are not "additional". By using the Bitcoin network, one is using a fully electrified technology in preference to two far more emission intensive industries: [[114|The Banking system]] (as a method of transacting), and [[115|the Gold mining]] (as a [[116|store of value]]).
101: A balanced evaluation of Bitcoin mining, as with any emerging climate technology, requires assessing both its current footprint and its future potential. Early solar investments paved the way for today’s carbon-negative PV industry. In the same way, Bitcoin mining’s ability to fund renewable infrastructure, eliminate methane emissions, and stabilize grids may ultimately yield net reductions far exceeding its operational emissions. Policymakers and environmental stakeholders must adopt this balanced lens, looking not only at current emissions but future potential. A good rule of thumb is this. If our rubric for evaluating a nascent technology's climate impact would have resulted in solar panels being banned in the 1990s (when the photovoltaic industry created considerably more emissions than it abated), then it is likely to be a bad methodology.
103: **First**, Bitcoin mining directly tackles renewable energy bottlenecks. By monetizing stranded power, miners reduced interconnection queues in [[117|Texas]] and [[118|Ethiopia]], enabling wind farms like US Bitcoin Corp's 280 MW Texas project, while cutting curtailment fees. [[119|Jaichi West ]]for example found that just a 4% reduction of curtailment led to a 12% increase in profitability. In one peer-reviewed model, a solar farm's payback period fell from 8.1 years to 3.5 years [[120|when paired with mining]], and [[121|mining gives wind farms a revenue floor]]. This has led Germany's largest Telco, Deutsche Telekom, and Japan's largest Utility, Tepco, to start using Bitcoin mining for their previously wasted renewable energy.
107: Critics who dismiss these efforts as “[[123|greenwashing]]” overlook the sheer volume and scale at which Bitcoin mining is now measurably enabling climate action across multiple areas. They also overlook the hard data: 61.5% of the Bitcoin mining companies we track now use >98% sustainable energy (network-wide, Cambridge puts the sustainable share at 52.4%), and carbon-negative mining (29 companies) already offsets 7% of the network’s emissions. Projects like Virunga National Park—which credits Bitcoin mining for saving its 7,800 km² rainforest and funding anti-poaching and deforestation efforts—show that Bitcoin mining’s value extends beyond energy systems to biodiversity preservation.
108: To policymakers and NGOs: the evidence is clear. Bitcoin mining is no longer a hypothetical solution—it is already resolving, at scale, the grid instability issues that come with higher concentrations of solar/wind energy. It is also electrifying parts of rural Africa, and funding OTEC breakthroughs. Rejecting Bitcoin mining's contribution to climate action risks prolonging reliance on gas peakers, methane flaring, and methane venting. In the race to net-zero, Bitcoin mining is not optional—it’s operational. Let's embrace it, research it, and leverage its unique ability to solve some of the toughest roadblocks en route to our Net Zero Emission goals.
